On the night of Ramchandra Ray's escape Udayaditya confronts Sitaram at the locked inner-quarters door, orders him to open it, draws his sword on him and has Sitaram disarm himself and be bound with his own cloth before leaving; on the night of Udayaditya's prison escape Sitaram opens Udayaditya's prison door, tells him the prison is on fire, grabs him and carries him out, and then leads him away asking him to come with him.

Pratapaditya’s initial plan was to have two Pathan men kill Basanta Ray when he took shelter at the inn in Simultali on his way to Jessore. The plan failed. Basanta Ray is finally killed by sword execution in Raigarh: on Pratapaditya’s signed order Muktiyar Khan has Abdul come in with a drawn sword and strike him, with blood flowing in the room.

The Mahishi’s room/inner quarters while disguised as a middle-aged woman/Mother Nikasha, and the king’s chamber/palace room where Ramai Bhand is present as the jester and is grabbed by the scruff of the neck and thrown out of the room.
Surma is covertly poisoned to death — a poison prepared by Mangala, who is Rukmini, and secretly obtained for the Rajmahishi by Matangini, causes her to die before she can be exiled.

Ramchandra Ray is insulted by her refusal and takes revenge by marrying another woman, so when Vibha finally reaches Chandradwip she finds the Maharaj is getting married and has no place or home for her in the royal palace.

Udayaditya gives his signet ring to Rukmini when she demands it. The ring has a seal with the Yubaraj’s name engraved on it. Rukmini keeps the ring and it is used by Sitaram and Bhagavat to stamp a forged petition that purports to be a complaint of treason by the Yubaraj against Pratapaditya. Bhagavat presents the forged, stamped petition to Pratapaditya as evidence, and on the basis of that petition Pratapaditya orders Udayaditya imprisoned.

Ramchandra Ray’s midnight escape makes Pratapaditya begin to pay special attention to Udayaditya, so news about Udayaditya reaches the Maharaj immediately. Pratapaditya learns that Udayaditya has fixed a monthly stipend for the dismissed guards Sitaram and Bhagavat. Udayaditya tells Surma about the order stopping the stipends and the need to help the guards secretly. Surma arranges for the stipends to be sent to Sitaram’s mother and Bhagavat’s wife through a trusted maid, but the maid does not keep the matter secret from Mangala. The word of the secret stipends reaches Pratapaditya’s ears, and he sends an order to the inner quarters that Surma must go to her paternal home.

The song is an expression of profound loneliness, grief and emptiness at being the sole survivor left behind after those he loved have gone; a lament that what was there has gone away and what remains is only emptiness.

Basanta Ray sings it first in Raigarh in the afternoon on his palace veranda, alone gazing at the setting sun over a mango grove, humming the song to himself in nostalgic melancholy about his absent loved ones in Jessore and the loss of joy in singing.

He sings it again in Jessore in the inner quarters of the royal palace with Vibha, after seeing the empty Surma’s room and being told no one is there, standing in the silent desolate household; he takes Vibha’s hand and slowly sings the song as a shared lament for the shattered family and for Udayaditya’s imprisonment.

Rukmini fails to stop Udayaditya’s midnight escape and later tells Pratapaditya that the Yubaraj escaped with the old king of Raigarh and that Sitaram, Basanta Ray and Udayaditya conspired. On Rukmini’s information Pratapaditya learns Udayaditya is in Raigarh and sends Muktiyar Khan to Raigarh with a secret order. Muktiyar Khan captures Udayaditya and, on Pratapaditya’s signed order, has Basanta Ray executed.

Pratapaditya initially received Ramchandra Ray with deliberate, cool indifference — refusing to send a proper welcome, not lighting the path, not playing the Nabat, and when they met receiving him without joy or haste, interrupting him and sending him to the inner quarters, a reception that made Ramchandra understand Pratapaditya’s superiority; later Ramchandra addresses Pratapaditya’s status in his own court by publicly humiliating and mocking him, with daily verbal attacks from ministers and jesters about Pratapaditya’s lineage and the need for anointment by Ramchandra’s grandfather, treating Pratapaditya as inferior and using the court to ridicule him.

The older widow is Rukmini, who left Raigarh, changed her name to Mangala and lives on the outskirts of Jessore. She befriends palace servants and keeps news of the palace. The Rajmahishi, hearing that the widow Mangala knows tantra, mantra and medicine, sends Matangini to secretly fetch medicine from her. Mangala spends the night cutting, soaking, grinding and chanting mantras to prepare a poison and performs rituals so that Udayaditya would feel no pity when Surma dies. Surma dies by poison in the palace.

Udayaditya’s early wish not to have been born crown prince and to be freed from the burden of the kingdom leads, after his capture, to his appearance before Pratapaditya as a prisoner. He declares he is not worthy of the kingdom and pleads to be released from the throne, naming Samaraditya as heir. Pratapaditya demands proof of his feeling; Udayaditya then goes to the temple and, in Pratapaditya’s presence, touches the feet of Ma-Kali and swears an oath that as long as he lives he will not accept even an iota of the Maharaja of Jessore’s kingdom as his own, will not sit on the throne of Jessore and will not even touch the royal scepter of Jessore, and takes the sin of his grand-uncle’s murder upon himself if he ever does. He then asks to be allowed to leave for Kashi instead of being locked up, to establish a guest house and temple there in his grand-uncle’s name.

Ramchandra Ray handed the spiteful letter to Nayanchand to take to Jessore. Nayanchand was afraid of what Pratapaditya might do if the letter reached him and resolved to give the letter to the Mahishi instead of delivering it. The Mahishi kept the letter secret, did not tell Vibha and did not tell Pratapaditya that the letter had actually been written. 

Later the Mahishi showed the letter to Basanta Ray. Basanta Ray read it and, believing Ramchandra had written it only out of anger, said the Mahishi should not show the letter to anyone else and should send Vibha to her father-in-law’s house at once, and that Ramchandra’s anger would subside once she was sent back. He said to announce in the household that Ramchandra had written a letter requesting that Vibha be sent to Chandradwip.

The Mahishi then told Vibha and announced throughout the household that Ramchandra Ray had written a letter requesting that Vibha be sent to her in-laws’ house, the opposite of the letter’s actual content which renounced Vibha and said she should not be sent to Chandradwip again.

The canal blocking with large sal logs only stops the boat briefly; Rammohan and his followers pull the boat up and over the logs, and the guards fail to intercept in time because they have no guns or gunpowder, cannot find a flintlock, and the man sent to fetch a chase boat delays by stopping for tobacco and to collect a debt.

In Chapter 13 Basanta Ray picks up his sitar and begins to play it furiously with a great clatter, but seeing Vibha’s tears his playing is greatly hindered, his eyes keep blurring with tears, his throat becomes choked and he has to stop playing and put the sitar down. He leaves it behind saying “I am leaving this sitar behind, Dada, I will not play it anymore.” In Chapter 27 his eternal companion, the sitar, is no longer with him and he says “It’s not that I don’t have the sitar. The sitar is there, only its strings have broken, and it can no longer be tuned.”

Earlier he would intervene to protect oppressed subjects and fight oppression without considering consequences; after Surma’s death he is seized by fear of Pratapaditya, hesitates in every task, does not stop officials from beating subjects, turns away from looting reports and does not send help to Bhagavat and Sitaram, no longer willing to intervene on their behalf.
He opens Udayaditya’s prison door during the fire and leads the imprisoned Yubaraj out to freedom.

First desperate occasion: Rammohan ties several thick sheets together into a huge rope, ties it to a small pillar on the palace roof above the south-side canal, lifts Ramchandra Ray onto his back, climbs down the rope about seventy cubits to the sixty-four-oared boat below, grips the rope with his teeth at the end, releases Ramchandra from his back and lowers him with both hands into the boat before jumping down himself.

Second desperate occasion: after Vibha faints in Ramchandra Ray’s presence, Rammohan lifts the unconscious and exhausted Vibha, brings her out of the palace, places her into a palanquin at the gate and takes her to the boat for departure to Kashi with Udayaditya.

In Jessore, when preparing to receive Ramchandra Ray, Vibha is dressed by the Mahishi in heavy royal finery — eight thick gold bangles and one huge diamond bracelet on each arm, a large nose ring, and an imposed coiffure — carrying the burden of her coiffure, nose ring and arms full of bangles with unruly joy showing in her eyes and face. 

In Chandradwip, when she finally seeks him out, she steps out from the boat dressed as a common woman, like a beggar-woman, refusing a palanquin and saying she will go like a common subject, and enters the palace like any other maidservant with a veil over her head.

In his bedchamber after Surma’s death the window is the empty spot where Surma used to sit and the place he goes with the flicker of hope that opening the door he will see Surma sitting there; it frames the same moonlight, garden and breeze and prompts the thought “on such an evening, how could Surma possibly stay away?” and is linked to hearing a voice like Surma’s and looking for her, a site of memory, longing and imagined return.

In the prison cell the small casement is a two hands’ breadth opening onto a sliver of sky, a bamboo grove and a Shiva temple, with fireflies, birds and passing travelers visible through it. Sitting by it he stays awake listening to the guards; from it he can see the sky and the birds fly and he thinks “my cage too will one day break, and I too will one day swim in that endless sky to my heart’s content, just like those birds.” Away from the window he sees only darkness and forgets he will be free; at the window “I know that I am naturally free; no king or emperor can hold me captive,” while the soft bed in the room is his prison.

The arrangement begins as flirtatious and financial: Rukmini, a widow who lends money at interest, holds Sitaram under her control with beauty and silver. Sitaram, penniless, visits her for money, jokes about needing alms and gold and silver, and is given money on the promise of repayment. Their exchanges are playful, with Sitaram calling her Subhadra and himself Jagannath, responding to her prompts “Pran,” “Priye,” “Priyatame,” “Pranpriye,” and joking about interest.

The financial tie sours as Sitaram’s memory of repayment vanishes, his visits become frequent and secretive, and they confer secretly about a matter that requires Bhagavat’s help. When Udayaditya is imprisoned, Sitaram goes to Rukmini’s house, curses her, threatens to set her house on fire, grind her face on the stone floor, smear her with lime and soot and drive her from the city, and says he will free the Yubaraj. Rukmini listens, her hatred gathers, and she declares the Yubaraj is hers and only she can do him good or harm.

Later Sitaram is involved in the palace fire and the burning of Udayaditya’s prison cell. He returns to Jessore at night intending to steal money from Rukmini, believing Mangala is dead. He finds her cottage door open, enters a dark house, and finds Rukmini in her bedroom sitting with sleepless eyes, trembling violently, wet cloth around her half-covered body, water dripping from disheveled hair, her face ashen. He mocks her. She stands and vows she has returned from Yama’s door, will lay him and the Yubaraj in the oven, smear her body with ash from their pyres, and then satisfy Yama’s desire.

Sitaram tries feigned affection; Rukmini’s rage intensifies, she looks for a curved blade, and Sitaram flees the cottage as she comes after him with the blade, striking the floor where he stood. He concludes it is unwise to stay in Jessore and flees that night with his family to Raigarh.

Sitaram helps start the guardhouse fire with a few commoners loyal to Udayaditya and some palace servants and places his men among those fighting the fire who pour water where there is no fire, fail to bring water back, break water pots and create confusion so the fire will not go out. The blaze and the resulting chaos lets the guards run off and lets Sitaram take Udayaditya out of prison. While the chaos is unfolding Sitaram’s men set fire to Udayaditya’s empty prison cell, setting windows, doors, beams, rafters, doorframes and wooden fences ablaze. Sitaram returns to the palace from the boat, takes Udayaditya’s sword and the letters, keeps only the letters for the Mahishi and Vibha and destroys the remaining one, and throws bones, a skull and Udayaditya’s sword into the burning cell. Shouts are raised that the Yubaraj’s cell has caught fire, that the Yubaraj was heard screaming inside, and Sitaram cries that the roof has collapsed and there is no response from him. The cell burns, collapses and is entered only after the fire, and the burnt remains of the sword are produced as evidence, so the rumor spreads that the Yubaraj died in the fire.

Ramchandra Ray does not show gratitude for Udayaditya’s rescue; he treats the rescue as something that was bound to happen and believes Udayaditya acted mainly for his sister’s sake, not for Ramchandra himself. In court he brings up Udayaditya’s name alongside Pratapaditya’s to laugh and joke with ministers and courtiers, joining in the ridicule and mockery of Udayaditya for the crime of being Pratapaditya’s son, and lets the tearing down of imaginary figures of Pratapaditya and Udayaditya continue without stopping it.

A forged petition stamped with the Yuvraj’s seal is made to appear as if Prince Udayaditya is lodging a complaint of treason against Pratapaditya with the Emperor of Delhi, and Bhagavat brings that petition to Pratapaditya saying it was intercepted from a servant of Udayaditya on his way to Delhi.

In Chapter 8 Vibha secretly goes to Surma and has her hair done to her own liking, so Surma’s styling of Vibha’s hair marks Surma’s caring presence in the Jessore palace. After Surma is gone, in Chapter 18 Vibha sits quietly at the time to braid her hair as if Surma will come at any moment to braid it for her and waits for her, but evening falls, night approaches and Surma does not come and her hair remains unbraided. Surma never fails to come when Vibha is sad, but now even if her heart breaks she will not come. Later Rammohan notes Vibha’s hair is unkempt, showing the absence of Surma’s grooming.
